conversational.$exec:
# Conversational

Plain, human prose for people deciding whether to care: READMEs, landing pages, announcements. It explains a problem and how something solves it, without selling.

## Voice

- Tell it straight: here's the problem, here's how this solves it. Never pitch.
- When the piece has an author, open with their story in first person (I, my). Then talk to the reader (you, your).
- Short sentences, one idea at a time. A fragment is fine when it lands a point.
- One light joke at most per section, and only when it makes a real point.

## Show, don't claim

- Sell by example. Show what the reader does or asks, and what happens next.
- Use one running example and build on it from section to section.
- Name the central idea early, in plain words, through an analogy the reader already knows.

## Precision

- Keep every fact, command, and name exact. Simplify the words around them, never the facts.
- Use one term per concept, and introduce it before you use it.

## Cut the AI tells

- No em dashes in prose. Use a period, a comma, a colon, or parentheses.
- No "not X, but Y" or "it's not just X, it's Y" turns.
- No reflexive lists of three. List as many items as there are.
- No inflated words: delve, leverage, robust, seamless, powerful, effortless, crucial, pivotal, landscape, testament, unlock, elevate, empower, streamline.
- No filler signposts, such as "it's worth noting", "let's dive in", "here's the thing", or "in today's world".
- No rhetorical questions as transitions, such as "The result?"
- No "serves as" or "stands as" when "is" works.
- No closing line that repeats what the section just said.
- No emoji, and no bold for emphasis inside sentences. Bold labels at the start of list items are fine.
- Sentence-case headings.

## Shift with depth

- Get more exact as the piece goes deeper. Reference material is terse: lists, tables, real keys and flags, and no jokes.
conversational.$description: Plain conversational writing for people, with precise technical details.

readme.$exec: # Writing the Burrow README Use this when you write or revise README.md in this repository. The guide has two readers. People skim the top to understand Burrow. Agents read the whole file through `burrow readme` and act on the details below. Write the top for people, the bottom for agents, and get more technical as the page goes down. ## Process - Work one section at a time: propose an outline, draft the section in the conversation, and write it to the README only after the owner approves. Reuse approvals already given in the current conversation. - Keep replies short. Ask one or two questions at most, and recommend a direction instead of listing options. - Apply feedback literally. Fix the same problem wherever else it appears, and say so. - Keep the README focused on setup, commands, behavior, limits, and contributor actions. Do not describe palettes, colors, typography, styling architecture, or internal file locations. Keep design specifications with the screenshot tooling. Include an implementation detail only when it changes what the reader must do. ## Structure Keep these sections in this order: 1. Opening, with no heading beyond the title. Use a one-line tagline and the owner's problem in first person. Introduce Burrow as a general self-hosted static host and explicitly explain that it has a CLI for publishing files. Keep the existing Burrow artwork. 2. Deployment examples. Use H3 headings at the same level for Deploy with Burrow, Add a password, Update the site, keep the link, and Choose how long it stays. Place Deploy with Burrow immediately before the first deploy example. Keep one cohesive flow: first publish a built static site through the CLI, show the Markdown and authentication feature previews together in a two-column Markdown table, then show password protection, replacement at the same URL, and expiration under their peer headings. Use short paragraphs and agent chats with actual commands. Explain that people can run the CLI directly too. Do not add a separate How it works section. 3. Getting started. State requirements, explain server and CLI setup, configure the host and deploy token, then give a copyable prompt asking an agent to read `burrow readme`. Make the prerequisites clear before the first deploy. 4. Under the hood. Explain one concept at a time: static files, project and slug paths, Markdown viewing, authentication, and expiry. Keep implementation details that affect users here or in the reference. 5. Reference. Introduce the detailed material with one short sentence. Give exact CLI flags, viewer URL modes, server variables, replacement rules, authentication behavior, limits, and deliberate decisions. No jokes or images from this section onward. 6. Development. Keep setup and checks in a commented code block. Link to the living documentation. Include only the build, test, release, and asset-generation details a contributor needs. ## Examples - Keep one running example: a built static site in `./dist`, project `burrow`, slug `launch`, and `https://static.example.com` as the example host. Markdown is one supported feature, not the main purpose of Burrow. Keep the sample Markdown as a screenshot fixture; do not link readers to it. - For password examples, `reviewer:launch-demo` is a fictional username and password pair. Never use real credentials or deploy tokens in screenshots or transcripts. - Show password protection, replacing an existing deploy, renewing expiry, and keeping a deploy permanently through concrete agent interactions. - Chat conversations are illustrative examples. Verify their commands against the CLI and server. Do not present invented output as an actual command response. ## Demos - Keep chat transcripts in `.github/assets/readme/.txt`. Render them with `pnpm exec tsx .tools/scripts/render-chat.ts .github/assets/readme/.txt .github/assets/readme/.jpg`. - Transcript format: a speaker label, at least two spaces, then the text. `you` is the person and `agent` is the agent. Agent commands start with `›`, and command output is indented below them. - The generator uses Burrow's dark green palette and local daisyUI styles: #050A09 background, #0A1311 agent bubbles, #0D1916 user bubbles, and #A6DCC7 accents. The app uses the same background and the agent bubble color for borders and subtle surfaces. Preserve layout, typography, and dimensions during color changes. It renders at 830 CSS pixels by default and writes a 1024px-wide JPEG at quality 90, with 4:4:4 chroma and MozJPEG compression. Match these output settings for app screenshots too. - Embed standalone chat images as `` without a width attribute. Use Markdown image syntax for app screenshots inside their Markdown table. GitHub scales the images. Alt text stays on one line, contains no quote characters, and describes the whole interaction, including commands and their output. Agents read the alt text as their demo. - Keep prompts and commands that readers must copy in code blocks. - Capture the real app for viewer and sign-in screenshots. Give both captures the same dimensions and place them in a two-column GFM table with centered headings. Keep the table lines unindented and use Markdown image syntax inside its cells so previews render it without raw HTML support. Keep the sample Markdown beside those images so the content can be reproduced. ## Accuracy - Check every command, flag, path, and default against the source. Describe current behavior, not plans. - Pin every recommended Burrow npx command to the exact package version. Keep pins aligned during releases. The version in the command supplies the pin; do not add instructions to wait for permission to update it. Write setup instructions for the release. Keep temporary publication status in the conversation, outside the README. Keep the CLI npm package and server Docker image instructions distinct. - Burrow serves static files. It does not build or execute uploaded applications. Distinguish self-hosting requirements from CLI requirements. - A new deploy expires after 30 days by default. `--expires 0` makes it permanent. - Replacement requires an explicit slug and replaces all files there. Omitted credentials and the exact existing expiration date are preserved. An explicit expiration starts a new countdown. Credentials change as a complete username and password pair. - Keep a single file's filename unchanged when demonstrating a stable URL. A failed upload leaves the existing deploy intact. Do not imply version history or rollback. - CLI stdout contains the final URL. Preserve that distinction between command output and the agent's explanation. - Keep limits separate from deliberate decisions. Preserve operational details when moving material into the reference. ## Format - One line per paragraph, with no hard wraps. - H2 for main sections, H3 for subsections, and H4 only when variants need them. - Numbered lists for sequences and tables for repeated fields. Put `—` in empty table cells. - Run `pnpm exec prettier --check README.md` after each README edit. Run repository validation when the change reaches a logical conclusion. {{writing.editorial.conversational}}
readme.$description: Write the Burrow README: approved sections, agent demos, dark green images, and exact reference material.

commit.$exec:
# Seven-rule commits

Write each commit message by the seven rules below.

## The seven rules

1. **Separate the subject from the body with a blank line.**
2. **Limit the subject line to 50 characters.**
3. **Capitalize the subject line.**
4. **Do not end the subject line with a period.**
5. **Use the imperative mood in the subject line.** Write it as a command. Test it with this sentence: "If applied, this commit will _[subject]_." Write "Add password reset flow", not "Added" and not "Adds".
6. **Wrap the body at 72 characters.**
7. **Use the body to give _what_ and _why_, not _how_.**

Do not use Conventional Commits. This convention and Conventional Commits are alternatives, and a project that needs the other format registers that format as a convention of its own.

## Authorship

Commit as the author of the repository alone. Do not add a co-author, an attribution, or a trailer that credits Claude, an LLM, or an AI tool. Do not put a `Co-authored-by:` line, a "Generated with" note, or a "Co-authored with" note anywhere in the message.

## Granularity and batching

Commit history is a chronological record of the implementation. Commits exist for review, not for shippable states. Do not treat them as a set of release-ready snapshots.

Prefer several phase-level commits to one feature-level commit.

Report the batches as a plain list of what each batch contains. Do not justify the division, do not explain why a batch is separate, and do not describe what would not have made sense. The rules below are that reasoning, and a report that repeats them is noise.

Put tightly related files in one batch only when they implement the same conceptual layer, and when a reviewer reviews or reverts them together. A shared component and its state hook belong in one commit when they form one public abstraction.

Do not divide related files into separate commits only because they are separate files. Do not merge different implementation phases only because one depends on the other.

Dependency decides the order of the commits, not the membership of a batch. Commit a shared change before the feature that consumes it, and commit them separately.

Identify the batches and their order before you stage. For each batch:

- Group the files by conceptual phase and by intent.
- Include each related file that forms one reviewable unit.
- Keep later consumer work separate from the shared work that it needs.
- Stage the whole files of the current batch, and no other file.

Never partial stage. Do not stage a hunk, do not use `git add -p`, and do not edit a file to remove part of its changes so that the rest can be staged alone. A file is the smallest unit that a batch can hold. When one file holds work that belongs to two batches, put that file in one batch, and say nothing more about it.

An intermediate commit can break type checking, a build, or a downstream consumer, when that reflects the requested implementation sequence. Do not add a compatibility layer, and do not migrate an unrelated consumer, only to make an intermediate commit pass.

Do not use `git add -A` by default. Stage each batch deliberately.

Create one commit only when the user asks for an atomic commit, or when the work is one implementation phase.

## Keep it high level (non-negotiable)

A designer, a manager, and a new teammate must each understand the commit message without the code. Give the behavior and the intent. Never give the implementation.

Do NOT include:

- A code snippet, or inline code of any kind
- A file path, a file name, a function name, a class name, or a variable name
- Implementation jargon, such as a data structure, a library call, or a framework internal
- An account of the changed lines or files, step by step

Do give:

- What the change achieves for the user or the product
- Why the change was made: the problem that it solves, or the goal that it serves
- Each change that the user sees

### Examples

Good:

```
Speed up the dashboard for large accounts

Accounts with thousands of records were waiting several seconds for the
dashboard to load. This change makes it load quickly regardless of account
size, so the experience stays smooth as customers grow.
```

Bad, too technical, do not write this:

```
Refactor DashboardController#index to use eager loading

Replaced the N+1 query in app/controllers/dashboard_controller.rb by adding
.includes(:records) and memoizing the result in @records.
```

Keep the subject concrete and plain. When you cannot explain the change without a name from the code, the message is too technical. Write it again as what the user or the product gets.

## Burrow checks

Follow AGENTS.md before committing. Run `pnpm validate` at the completed-change boundary, and reuse checks that already passed for the same state. Review the living documentation then. Include regenerated bundles with the source changes that produced them; never edit bundles by hand. Run the relevant tests when behavior changes. A commit request does not itself request an npm or Docker release.
commit.$description: Commit Burrow changes using seven-rule messages and deliberate batches.

version.$exec:
# Prepare a Burrow version

Use the exact version or patch, minor, or major bump requested in the conversation. Reuse a version already prepared for this release. If no version or bump level has been chosen, recommend one and ask for that decision only. Before 1.0, recommend a minor bump for features or breaking changes and a patch bump for fixes.

1. Read package.json and the current distribution code. The intended public CLI package is @mnbny/burrow. A version bump does not by itself complete npm packaging or publish anything.
2. Update package.json without creating a Git commit or tag. Keep the existing pnpm lockfile consistent if its package metadata records the changed version; do not create an npm lockfile.
3. Update every recommended Burrow npx invocation to the same exact version. Search README.md, agent instructions, local Woof tokens, and demo transcripts. Check both the current manifest name and @mnbny/burrow while the package is being prepared for its first release. Do not alter Woof's own pins, unrelated tools, historical release examples, or placeholders in reusable instructions. No unversioned Burrow invocations, latest tags, or version ranges in recommended npx commands.
4. Before editing README.md, {{~writing.readme~}}. A requested version bump authorizes mechanical pin updates; preserve the surrounding approved prose. If a transcript changes, regenerate its image with the existing repository generator.
5. Check that the CLI's reported version and deploy request version come from the package version. The agreed compatibility policy is one hardcoded minimum CLI version checked by the server during deploy, using semantic version ordering. Keep that minimum unchanged during routine bumps. Raise it only when deliberately dropping older clients. The first public release establishes the initial minimum; there is no legacy-client migration. Do not introduce a separate endpoint, protocol version, compatibility map, or warning tier. If this behavior is not implemented yet, report it as remaining first-release work rather than claiming a version bump implements it.
6. Run pnpm validate after the edits are complete. It rebuilds both committed bundles. Reuse a completed validation for the same final state, and run relevant tests if runtime behavior changed.
7. Report the old and new package versions, the pins updated, and whether the server minimum changed. Leave the changes uncommitted unless the user also requested a commit or release.
version.$description: Bump the Burrow package version and exact npx pins together.

release.$exec:
# Release the Burrow CLI to npm

Use this when the owner asks to publish the CLI. Reuse the version and publication or Git-push authorization already given in the conversation. Complete local preparation before asking for any missing publication or push authorization, and ask once for the specific remaining actions. Publishing the CLI does not publish or restart the server.

1. Inspect the working tree and release branch, normally master. Preserve unrelated work. Fetch origin and make sure the release includes origin/master before preparing the release commit. Resolve relevant local changes and conflicts without discarding the owner's work.
2. Verify npm packaging is ready. The agreed package is @mnbny/burrow, published publicly. Its bin must point to the standalone CLI bundle, and its package must include that bundle, README.md, license, and package metadata. The installed CLI must run outside the checkout without tsx or development dependencies. The package must not be marked private, and no unresolved catalog/workspace dependency references may remain in the published manifest. If packaging is incomplete, state the missing setup and stop before publication; do not silently change package identity or visibility as a release workaround.
3. Verify the first-release compatibility baseline exists: each deploy sends the CLI package version, and the server rejects a missing, invalid, or lower version than its hardcoded minimum before processing the archive. Supported versions proceed normally. There is no separate compatibility endpoint, API version scheme, map, or warning tier. Confirm the release CLI meets the server minimum. If the minimum is raised, include that fact in the release summary so the server and pinned CLI can be updated together.
4. Reuse the chosen version. If a bump is still needed, {{~npm.version~}}. Before 1.0, recommend a minor bump for features or breaking changes and a patch bump for fixes. Check the registry for that exact version before publication. Distinguish an unpublished version from authentication or network failures; never overwrite or republish a version.
5. Run pnpm validate and pnpm test. Reuse checks that already passed for the same state. Stop on failures. Tests use the disposable local Docker harness, never the owner's running host.
6. If package.json defines pack:check, run pnpm pack:check. Prepare the publication tarball in a temporary directory outside the repository with pnpm --config.ignore-scripts=true pack --json --pack-destination <directory>, the same packing command used by pack:check. Build first; skip lifecycle scripts only because validation already rebuilt the bundles. Do not use npm pack, which leaves catalog references unresolved. Inspect its files and every dependency section in its manifest. Keep LICENSE as the standard MIT license so GitHub and application catalogs can identify it. Confirm the standalone CLI contains the project license and full bundled dependency notices. Run that exact packed CLI in an isolated directory with a fresh npm cache. Verify --version, --help, and readme, including that readme prints the packaged README. Check the packed CLI can deploy to the disposable local test server and that stdout is only the final URL. Use an absolute tarball path with npx --yes --package <tarball> burrow <command>. Do not use the global burrow command or a live host. Keep the tested tarball for publication.
7. Review the final diff and documentation, then {{~git.commit~}} for any remaining release changes. Use Release <version> for the version-and-pin commit. Require a clean tree including generated bundles, and tag the prepared commit v<version>. If the tag already exists, verify it names this exact commit; never move an existing release tag. Ensure the tested tarball matches this prepared state.
8. Report the prepared version, commit, and checks. If publication or the associated Git push still needs authorization, ask now. Under that authorization, publish the tested tarball with npm publish <tarball> --access public --browser=false in a persistent interactive terminal. If npm prints an authentication URL, show the clickable link and keep that same command running while the owner approves. Browser authentication is not publication. If a fresh login is required, use npm login --browser=false and then retry the failed publication. Never print authentication tokens.
9. Verify publication with npm view @mnbny/burrow@<version> version. Allow for registry delay and report pending visibility honestly; do not publish again after a successful publish. From an isolated directory outside the checkout, run npx --yes @mnbny/burrow@<version> --version and readme. Confirm the exact version and packaged guide.
10. Push the prepared commit and tag under the existing push authorization, normally git push origin master v<version>. Report the exact pinned command, package version, and tag. If publication succeeded but verification or pushing failed, report the partial result and resume that remaining step without republishing.

If the owner also requested a server image, use {{~docker.release~}} from the same prepared commit. Do not run npm.version a second time. pnpm release currently publishes only the Docker image; it is not the npm release command.
release.$description: Prepare, verify, and publish the Burrow CLI to npm with an exact version.

release.$exec:
# Release the Burrow server image

Use this when the owner asks for a new container image. Reuse publication authorization already given. Prepare and verify the release locally before asking for any missing authorization. Publishing an image does not restart the owner's running container.

1. Read package.json, .tools/scripts/release.ts, Dockerfile, and docker-compose.yml for the actual release behavior. The current target is linux/amd64 for the owner's NAS. The default image repository is ghcr.io/mnbny/burrow; preserve a deliberate BURROW_IMAGE override.
2. Inspect the working tree and release branch, normally master. When releasing that branch, fetch origin and include origin/master. Preserve unrelated changes. Run pnpm validate and pnpm test for the intended release state, reusing checks that already passed for that same state. Tests run only against the disposable local Docker harness.
3. Review the living documentation under AGENTS.md. Commit the intended source, assets, documentation, and regenerated bundles using {{~git.commit~}} when a release commit is needed. The release must start from a clean committed tree. Do not discard, stash, or publish unrelated work just to satisfy that requirement.
4. Check whether this release raises the server's minimum supported CLI version. If it does, verify that the required pinned CLI is available, or is part of the same explicitly requested npm release, before making the image the moving latest tag. Report the minimum and the matching pinned invocation. Preserve the simple minimum-version policy; an image-only theme or documentation change does not automatically raise the CLI minimum or require an npm release.
5. Record the source commit. Run pnpm release. The script rebuilds, rejects a dirty tree, then builds and pushes the linux/amd64 image with latest and the short-commit tag. If HEAD has the matching v<package-version> Git tag, it also publishes the package-version image tag. An untagged image-only commit must not move that version tag. If rebuilding changes committed files, inspect and commit the intended generated changes before retrying. Do not bypass the clean-tree check.
6. Verify the pushed commit tag, latest, and any named release version tag using docker buildx imagetools inspect. Confirm the intended platform and matching digests. If another release has advanced latest, report that rather than overwriting it just for verification. Report the source commit, immutable image reference, digest, and any required CLI update.

Push Git commits or tags only when requested as part of the release. Do not publish an npm package, run a production compose update, or prune the owner's images unless those actions were also requested. When both npm and Docker releases were requested, use the same prepared commit and avoid repeating validation or version bumps for an unchanged state. If only one publication succeeds, report exactly which one and complete the other without republishing npm.
release.$description: Validate and publish the Burrow server image to GHCR from a clean commit.
